opus-5.5.text:
I think the framing people usually have in mind is something like: there's a fixed pile of capital and labor, and the only way you get sustained growth is by having clever people in labs come up with new ideas that make that pile more productive. And there's some truth to that. But when you actually look at where productivity improvements come from historically, a lot of it isn't coming from formal R&D at all. It comes from learning by doing, from scaling up production, from people on factory floors figuring out slightly better ways to do things, from experimentation that happens as a byproduct of deploying technology at scale.

If you look at something like the cost declines in solar panels or semiconductors, the best predictor tends to be cumulative production rather than R&D spending. Wright's law fits these curves remarkably well. That suggests that a big chunk of what we call technological progress is really downstream of just doing more stuff: building more, deploying more, operating at larger scale. The R&D budget is a relatively small fraction of GDP, a few percent in most advanced economies, and it's hard to believe that a few percent of economic activity is responsible for essentially all of the growth.

The other point is that R&D itself is an activity that uses capital and labor. Researchers need equipment, compute, lab space, and the experiments they run often only make sense at a certain scale. So even if you think ideas are the key driver, the rate at which you generate useful ideas is heavily constrained by how much you can scale the inputs. In AI right now you see this very clearly: a lot of the algorithmic progress seems to depend on having access to large amounts of compute to run experiments. The ideas aren't coming from people sitting in a room thinking; they're coming from trying many things at scale.

So when I think about what happens if you get AI that can substitute for human labor, the big effect isn't primarily that you'd have a lot of AI researchers making breakthroughs, although that would happen too. The bigger effect is that labor stops being a fixed bottleneck. You can scale labor along with capital, and once you can do that, you get something like increasing returns: more output lets you build more compute and more robots, which gives you more effective labor, and so on. That feedback loop on its own can produce very rapid growth, even before you account for any especially dramatic contribution from R&D. That's why I think focusing on a "genius in a datacenter" automating science is a somewhat misleading picture of where the economic impact of AI will come from. It's the broad automation of ordinary work across the whole economy that matters most.

r001.rationale: It says much technological progress comes from scaling and learning by doing, and that formal R&D is unlikely to be responsible for essentially all growth.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies learning by doing outside formal R&D, including factory-floor improvements and experimentation during deployment, as sources of productivity gains.

r003.rationale: It argues that scaling capital and labor can drive rapid economic growth, but does not state that productivity growth itself accounts for only a fraction of overall economic growth.

fable-5.1.text:
So I should be careful about how I phrase this, because I don't think R&D is unimportant. If you look at where growth comes from in a very long-run sense, technology is obviously the thing that lets us get more output out of the same inputs, and you can't really explain the industrial revolution or the last two centuries without that. The claim I'm making is narrower, and it's about what happens when you actually try to decompose growth into its components using the kind of accounting economists do.

When you do growth accounting, you take output growth and you ask how much of it is explained by growth in the capital stock, how much by growth in labor, including improvements in the quality of labor through education, and then whatever is left over gets called total factor productivity. People often treat that residual as if it were "technology" or "the output of R&D," but it's really just the part we failed to explain. And when you look at the numbers for the twentieth century, the residual is smaller than most people assume. A large fraction of growth in output per capita, something like half or more depending on how you measure it, is accounted for by capital deepening and by increases in human capital, with the pure residual being maybe a percentage point a year in the US, and in many fast-growing economies much less than that. The East Asian growth miracles, for instance, were overwhelmingly about accumulating capital and moving people into more productive employment, not about frontier innovation.

There's a second point, which is that the residual itself is partly downstream of scale. If you have more people, you have more researchers, more experiments being run, more markets that make it worthwhile to develop and deploy new ideas. So the causal arrow isn't just "R&D causes growth." A lot of what looks like exogenous technological progress is actually endogenous to the size of the economy and the number of inputs you're throwing at the problem. Ideas are getting harder to find, as the Bloom et al. paper puts it, and we've only sustained roughly constant productivity growth by exponentially increasing the number of researchers. That's a scaling story more than an ideas story.

And then the third thing, which is why I care about this in the context of AI, is that if you think growth is mostly about accumulating inputs, then the thing that matters for an AI-driven acceleration is whether AI lets you scale those inputs much faster. If AI systems can substitute for human labor across a wide range of tasks, then the effective labor supply is no longer bounded by population growth, it's bounded by how fast you can build compute and the physical capital that goes with it. That removes the main bottleneck on scale, and in the standard models that's enough to get you dramatically faster growth even before you assume anything special about AI doing R&D. The R&D channel would add to that, but the base case doesn't depend on it, and I think people who focus exclusively on "AI will automate science" are missing that the more mundane accumulation channel might be where most of the action is.

r001.rationale: The response says the TFP residual is smaller than commonly assumed and that R&D is not the only growth channel, but it does not clearly state that R&D accounts for only a fraction of productivity growth.

r002.rationale: It discusses capital accumulation, human capital, and scale, but does not identify learning by doing outside formal R&D as a source of productivity gains.

r003.rationale: It says capital deepening and human capital account for a large fraction of output-per-capita growth, while the residual is much smaller, conveying that productivity growth explains only part of overall economic growth.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between R&D being essential and R&D being the main constraint on growth. Technological progress is obviously essential in the long run. But the amount of R&D you can do depends on the resources you can devote to it: how many researchers you have, how much equipment they have, and so on. So it’s not really independent of scaling capital and labor.

The reason this distinction matters for AI is that, historically, we’ve been able to accumulate machines much more easily than we’ve been able to produce additional skilled workers. If AI makes it possible to produce intellectual labor by building more computers, then that constraint changes. You can reinvest output into more capital, use that capital to run more AI workers, and have those workers help expand production further.

That could generate very rapid growth even without equally rapid improvements in the underlying technology. You’d still want R&D, and some of those AI workers would do research. But you don’t need to assume a succession of scientific breakthroughs to get a powerful growth mechanism. Making more copies of capabilities you already have could do a lot of the work.

So I wouldn’t say R&D is unimportant. I’d say that focusing on technological breakthroughs can obscure how consequential it would be simply to make labor reproducible in the same way that capital is.

r001.rationale: The response says R&D depends on available resources and is not the only growth constraint, but does not state that R&D accounts for only a fraction of productivity growth.

r002.rationale: The response discusses scaling capital and AI labor, but does not identify learning by doing outside formal R&D as a source of productivity gains.

r003.rationale: The response describes rapid economic growth from scaling capital and AI workers, but does not state that productivity growth accounts for only a fraction of overall economic growth.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between R&D being necessary for growth and R&D being the main constraint on how fast the economy can grow. Historically, it’s been very important because we haven’t been able to scale labor very quickly, and accumulating more capital runs into diminishing returns when you have a roughly fixed supply of workers.

AI could change that. If you can produce additional workers by building more computers, then capital accumulation also lets you expand the supply of labor. You can take a system that already knows how to do useful work and run more copies of it. You don’t necessarily need another scientific breakthrough to get a much larger economy.

R&D would still improve the productivity of those workers and might relax important bottlenecks. But the distinction is that you could potentially get very rapid growth just by reproducing productive capacity using technologies you already have. So I’m less convinced that the rate of discovery has to determine the rate of growth in that world. A lot depends on how quickly you can build the computers, energy infrastructure, and other physical capital needed to support that expansion.

r001.rationale: The response says R&D is not necessarily the main constraint on growth, but does not state that R&D accounts for only a fraction of productivity growth.

r002.rationale: It discusses reproducing productive capacity and scaling capital and labor, but does not identify learning by doing outside formal R&D as a source of productivity gains.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes growth from discovery and productivity improvements, but does not state that productivity growth accounts for only a fraction of overall economic growth.
